tagline: Follow the Fremont River from ranch country through rock fins to badlands.
intro: Highway 24 follows the Fremont River through ranching communities, red sandstone cliffs and the rock fins of Capitol Reef National Park. The road is paved, and a portion carries the Capitol Reef Scenic Byway designation in the Utah Scenic Byways program. Capitol Reef Country promotes the drive for its passage from the Fremont River valley through the Waterpocket Fold to the eastern desert mesas. The Fremont also supplies year-round irrigation to Rabbit Valley and Caineville, linking the road’s ranching country and desert settlements through the same river.

The route took shape in stages: the road from Sigurd to Hanksville became a state highway in Wayne County in 1910, followed by its Piute and Sevier County sections in 1912. The legislature assigned the number 24 in 1927; in 1935 the highway extended northeast toward Green River. A 1961 realignment bypassed Capitol Reef Road between Fruita and Caineville.

Traveling east from Loa and Bicknell, begin with ranch country and the marshlands of Bicknell Bottoms. Near Torrey, meadows give way to red cliffs; inside the park, the route passes Chimney Rock, The Castle and Fruita’s orchards. Beyond the park, gray and purple Mancos Shale badlands spread toward Caineville and Hanksville, with Factory Butte on the horizon.

moments.title: Loa
moments.text: Loa’s name connects this Wayne County town to Hawaii: a Mormon missionary returning from there named it for Mauna Loa. The county seat lies along State Route 24, and its post office has operated since 1879. Nearby Spring Creek rises four miles north of town, where the state fish hatchery is located.

moments.title: Fruita
moments.text: At the meeting of the Fremont River and Sulphur Creek, Fruita’s orchards remain under National Park Service care. Mormons led by Nels Johnson established the settlement as Junction in 1880. Its one-room school opened in 1896 and also held dances and religious services. Reading, writing and arithmetic formed the core of lessons; teachers also offered history or geography when they could. The Park Service renovated the schoolhouse in 1966; it survives along with the Gifford house and barn. The orchards contain about 2,500 trees, tended by a small crew that prunes, irrigates, replants and sprays them.

moments.title: Giles
moments.text: Giles depended on a river that eventually overwhelmed its irrigation works. Burgess family members moved into Blue Valley by 1883 and built a dam and irrigation canal by 1884. The settlement’s first name came from soil colored blue-gray by Bentonite clay and Mancos Shale. The town occupied both riverbanks, linked by a footbridge, though most residents lived on the south side. Renamed Giles in 1895, it grew to 200 people by 1900. Severe floods in 1909–1910 defeated efforts to maintain the dam, and residents left when they could no longer irrigate. By 1919 it was a ghost town; two rock buildings, foundations and old corrals remain.
